title: Gone with the Wind
synopsis: Tara, Georgia, 1861. War is coming. You are Scarlett, sharp and impossible. The man you want isn't the man who wants you.

nodes.text: April at Twelve Oaks, and the barbecue is spread across a lawn that other people cleared, on a table other people are still carrying trays to and from, in a house nobody paid a wage to build. You are sixteen and the best-looking woman on that lawn and you know it to the ounce. Then somebody mentions over the cobbler that Ashley will marry his cousin Melanie in the autumn.

choices.consequence: You spend the entire afternoon manoeuvring toward a corridor where you can get him alone. At no stage does the plan account for anything he might want.
You laugh at three separate boys' jokes with all your teeth showing and eat nothing whatsoever. Everyone agrees afterward that you were in remarkable spirits.

nodes.text: You get him behind a door and tell him you love him straight out, the way a person places a bet. He says he is fond of you and that Melanie is made the way he is made and you are not. So you slap him and put a china bowl into the fireplace, and a man rises off a couch you had believed was empty and remarks that you throw well.

choices.consequence: Your hand goes up well ahead of your judgment. He takes it without flinching, which is somehow worse than if he had shouted or slapped you back.
You leave with your chin high, which fools nobody at all, because the man on the couch watched the whole performance and is laughing at your back.

nodes.text: Rhett Butler: put out of Charleston, put out of West Point, barred from most front parlours in the county, and standing here regardless with a drink. He bows a shade too low on purpose and says he has never been troubled by the good opinion of ladies. He has seen precisely what you are, and alone in the state of Georgia he appears to like you the better for it.

choices.consequence: You hand him something sharp about his reputation and he accepts it like a gift. You have just informed him that you will make an interesting game.
You cut him dead in front of two witnesses, which delights him, and which he quotes back to you word for word in a hallway many years later.

nodes.text: Melanie's brother is a soft, astonished boy who cannot believe his luck, and you marry him inside a fortnight, in haste, so as to be married before Ashley is. He goes off with the regiment and dies in a camp in South Carolina of measles and then pneumonia without ever hearing a shot fired. At seventeen you are a widow in black crape with a son you did not want.

choices.consequence: You wear the black, keep the veil down, decline every invitation for a year, and spend each of those days quietly calculating the date the year ends.
You cannot make yourself perform it. The county decides you are hard, and the county is right, and being right about you will not stop it borrowing from you later.

nodes.text: Atlanta is a raw, unfinished city full of soldiers and it suits you exactly. You board with Melanie and Aunt Pittypat and roll bandages badly. The hospitals take the churches, then the warehouses, then the depot yard itself. Rhett runs the blockade for money and never pretends it is for anything else, and he brings you a hat out of Paris that is far too green for a widow.

choices.text: Dance with him at the bazaar
choices.consequence: You take the floor in mourning black in front of the whole city because a man bid gold for the privilege. Atlanta talks for a month. You have not felt this alive in a year.
You sit the reel out with your gloved hands folded and watch the other women turn under the lamps, and the wanting is so loud you are amazed nobody hears it.

nodes.text: Shells come down on Peachtree Street for a month and everyone who can go has gone. Melanie is a fortnight overdue and cannot be moved. Prissy, who assured you she knew all about babies, informs you on the stairs that she does not, and she is right to be terrified. No doctor will come; there are three hundred men lying on the depot platform. So it is you, a basin, and scissors.

choices.consequence: You do it yourself in the August heat with the windows rattling, and you resent her every minute of it, and you do not leave the room once.
You get as far as the front hall twice and climb back up the stairs both times, because going would mean saying out loud exactly what you were going out of.

nodes.text: Rhett turns up with a bony horse and a wagon that should not hold together, and drives you out through a city burning from its own ordnance stores, the sky over the depot gone white with it. Melanie is flat in the back with the baby. Prissy is beside her with her eyes shut. Paint blisters on the shopfronts you pass, and nobody in that wagon speaks for a mile.

choices.consequence: You hand him the reins and let him choose the streets, and he brings four people out through a fire on a horse that is dead before morning.
You fight him about the route the entire way out of town, largely to have something to do with your hands, and he lets you do it.

nodes.text: Somewhere past the Rough and Ready road he halts the wagon and announces that he is going to enlist tonight, at the very end, for a cause he has spent four years calling a swindle in your hearing. Then he kisses you, steps down, and walks off into the dark. You are left with a dying horse, a woman who cannot sit up, a newborn, a frightened girl and twenty miles.

choices.consequence: You scream everything you own at his back on an empty road and he does not turn around once. Nobody has ever walked away from you before tonight.
You sit a moment and concede that he brought you out of a burning city and asked nothing for it. Then you take up the reins, because conceding it does not drive the wagon.

nodes.text: The house is standing only because the Yankees used it for a headquarters. Everything else is gone: the stock, the cotton, the smokehouse, the fences pulled down for firewood. Your mother died of typhoid two days ago. Your father walks you out to the steps and asks pleasantly when Ellen is coming down. There is a jar of hominy in the kitchen and, apart from that, nothing.

choices.consequence: You start counting what is left before you have finished crying. By dark you have three people in the cotton and no earthly idea how to pick it yourself.
You give yourself one hour in your mother's room with the door shut. Everybody in the house hears you, nobody comes in, and you never do it again as long as you live.

nodes.text: You walk the fields at Twelve Oaks looking for anything at all, dig up a radish, eat it raw with the dirt still on it, and it comes straight back up. Face down in somebody else's ruined furrow, sick and shaking, you make yourself a promise about hunger: that you will do whatever the thing costs, and that you are never going to be in this field again.

choices.consequence: You say it out loud to an empty field and it holds for the rest of your life, and it is paid for, over forty years, by every person who ever loves you.
You aim lower on purpose: food this week, seed by March, the tax money before autumn. The small version is the one that actually carries Tara through the winter.

nodes.text: The tax bill on Tara is three hundred dollars and you have not got three. You go up to Atlanta to get it out of Rhett, who turns out to be in a Yankee jail and unable to sign anything at all. On the way home you meet your sister's fiance, who owns a store and a sawmill and has waited four patient years, and you tell him she is marrying somebody else.

choices.consequence: You take his mill and double it inside a year with two crews and a very hard mouth. Atlanta can forgive a widow anything except doing arithmetic in public.
You attempt keeping house for a fortnight and nearly lose your mind in the parlour. Frank finds you at the ledgers at midnight and never entirely recovers from it.

nodes.text: You drive the mill road alone, because you always drive the mill road alone, and two men come off the bank at the horse's head. Big Sam, who left Tara at the surrender and owes you nothing whatever now that the law says so, crosses the ditch, pulls them off you and gets you home. That night Frank puts on his coat, takes a pistol, and will not say where.

choices.consequence: You tell him to leave it to the law, and he looks at you as though you had asked him to be less of a man in front of witnesses. He goes anyway.
You let him keep his silence and his pistol and ask nothing about either, which is a way of already knowing and choosing not to have been told.

nodes.text: The men ride out on a shantytown past the edge of the city and burn what they find and shoot at whoever runs, and the people living there are freed families and poor whites who had nothing to do with any road. Frank takes a bullet through the head. Ashley comes back shot through the shoulder, and Rhett lies to a Yankee captain to keep the rest of them off a rope.

choices.consequence: You sit up alone and admit that you sent him out and that a whole settlement of people burned for the convenience of your driving. You never say it to another soul.
You get through the funeral, the ledgers, the store and the mill without looking directly at any part of it. Not looking takes work that never appears in any account book.

nodes.text: He comes the week after the funeral with a diamond the size of a knuckle and no pretence about any of it. He says he has wanted you for years and will not insult you by talking about your soul. You do the arithmetic openly in front of him: the mill, the store, Tara's taxes, your sisters, Wade. He watches you finish the sum and marries you anyway with his eyes wide open.

choices.consequence: You say yes for the money, and he knows it, and takes you to New Orleans regardless. He has decided he can outlast you, which is the nearest he ever comes to an error.
You keep him waiting three days for an answer you settled in the first minute. He tells you later that those three days cost you a great deal more than they cost him.

nodes.text: New Orleans, and he spends money on you the way other men breathe. Restaurants, dressmakers, a suite with its own piano and a balcony. He lets you eat until you are ill and never once mentions a field or a radish. For a month he is careful with you, and funny, and awake at three in the morning listening to you have the same dream about running through fog toward something.

choices.consequence: You catch him being gentle and file it away somewhere without opening it. Years later you go looking for that file and find it exactly where you left it, still sealed.
You accept the whole month as your due and think no more about it. He is watching to see whether you will ask him a single question about himself. You never do.

nodes.text: Eugenie Victoria, called Bonnie for the colour of her eyes, and from the first hour she belongs to him. He walks the floor with her at night, buys her a pony, carries her into every drawing room in Atlanta so the old women will forgive her the parents she got. You look at your third child and feel the same guarded thing you felt for the first two, and say nothing.

choices.consequence: You find you can manage it with this one, in bursts, and it frightens you badly, because loving a thing is a debt that cannot be cleared by working harder.
You leave her to Rhett and to Mammy and tell yourself the mill requires you. Bonnie learns before she can spell which parent comes when she calls out.

nodes.text: You are in the mill office with both hands on Ashley's shoulders when his sister comes through the door, and by that evening the whole town has a version of it. Melanie, who has been told everything by everybody, seats you at her right hand at her own party and dares Atlanta to say one word about it. She is not a fool. She has simply decided what she intends to be.

choices.consequence: You get four words into the apology and she stops you, because she will not have those words said in her house. You are not forgiven so much as covered over.
You take her arm and let her walk you the length of her own drawing room in silence, and you hate her a little for making you owe her something that size.

nodes.text: She is four years old and she wants the bar put up higher, and he puts it up higher, because he has never once been able to refuse her. The pony goes into it. Afterward he will not let them carry her out of the room and he sits with every lamp burning because she was frightened of the dark. At the door he says a thing to you that cannot be taken back.

choices.consequence: You put your hand on the door frame and try, and he lifts his head, and that look is the reason you stop trying for the next two years.
You go to your own room and shut the door, and the two of you grieve the same child separately, at opposite ends of a house with fourteen rooms in it.

nodes.text: She is very small in the bed. She was forbidden a second child for years and had one regardless, and now this. She holds your wrist and asks you to look after Ashley and the boy, and then, in the same breath and without opening her eyes, asks you to be kind to Rhett, because she saw what nobody else in Atlanta ever bothered to look at.

choices.consequence: You give her your word about Ashley in a room that smells of camphor. It is the one promise in your life you keep at your own expense, and it costs you everything.
You start telling her she isn't dying, which is the coward's answer, and she waits with her hand on your wrist until you say yes properly.

nodes.text: In the hall afterward Ashley cannot hold himself upright and says he does not know how to go on, and it is not a turn of phrase. You have spent twelve years certain he was a fine man trapped in the wrong marriage. He was not. That marriage was the thing holding him off the floor, and you were the daydream he permitted himself on the ride out to the mill.

choices.consequence: The whole structure comes down in roughly four seconds and leaves you standing in a hallway holding a coat you no longer have any use for.
You keep your eyes on the wallpaper because looking straight at him would finish it. It finishes anyway, on the walk home, in the rain, at the corner of Peachtree.

nodes.text: You come in wet and tell him the truth at last, the whole of it, in the correct order and far too late. He listens the way a man reads a timetable for a town he has already left. He says he is going down to Charleston to see whether anything there still has manners. You ask what is to become of you, and he answers you with perfect courtesy.

choices.consequence: You take hold of his coat in the hall and hear your own voice asking. It is the first genuinely humble minute of your life, and tonight it buys you nothing at all.
You stand still and let the front door close and do not make one sound, and it costs you more than the field and the radish and the tax bill put together.
You do neither. You sit down on the bottom stair in a soaked dress and begin, for the first time in thirty years, working out what it is you actually want.

nodes.text: You go home to red dirt and a house with the paint gone and begin again, this time with wages, contracts and a lawyer in Jonesboro. The people who work that land are paid and are free to leave, and a good many of them do, and you learn to be a harder landlord than you meant to become. You grow old there, respected considerably more than liked, and die in a field in your eighties still planning the following spring.

You find him in Charleston, and it takes years, and it does not go the way you rehearse it. There is no single scene, no night of forgiving. There is a long correspondence, then a visit, then another visit, then a house. What comes back is smaller and steadier than what you lost. You spend the remainder of it beside a man who knows precisely what you are, which turns out to be the thing you were starving for on that lawn.

You keep the mill, buy two more, and have your own name painted over the door where the whole town can read it. You travel: New York, then Liverpool, then further than either. You marry late and quietly, a man who needs no rescuing and no winning. At sixty you work out that you spent your life arguing with a sixteen-year-old on a lawn, and that she was frightened rather than wicked. You let her off. You let nearly everybody off.
